analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license with safety training and background checks to buy or receive any gun.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House on November 1, 2023, referred to the Judiciary Committee the same day, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it unlawful to buy or receive a firearm without a federal license. To get a license, a person would have to pass a written firearms-law test and a hands-on shooting test, submit fingerprints and undergo a background investigation, and specify the exact gun they intend to buy; each license would cover a single firearm and expire after five years. It would also require every private gun sale or transfer to go through a licensed dealer for a background check, and require sellers to report every transaction to the Attorney General within three business days. States with their own substantially similar licensing systems would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of gun violence — in homes, schools, and public places — if fewer high-risk people are able to buy guns. Communities in states without their own licensing laws would gain the most, since the federal floor would apply there. Licensed gun dealers would also gain a new stream of fee-paying business, because private sales would have to be processed through them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to gun violence; licensed dealers

how_it_helps.text: Every buyer would need a federal license that requires a written test on firearms laws and hands-on firing and accuracy testing before any purchase.

Applicants would undergo a full background investigation, submit fingerprints, and identify the specific firearm and seller; the Attorney General could deny a license to someone judged a significant danger to self or others based on factors including a history of violence, domestic violence or stalking orders, or drug trafficking, with judicial review available for denials.
Private sales between unlicensed people would no longer be allowed directly; a licensed dealer would have to take possession and run the transfer through the standard background-check process.

Sellers and transferors would have to report every firearm transaction to the Attorney General within three business days, and the Attorney General would revoke licenses of people later judged dangerous, with procedures to remove firearms upon revocation.

analysis.who_pays: Gun buyers and owners, who would pay fees and time costs for a training course, testing, fingerprinting, and a background investigation for every gun they acquire, with each license covering only one gun bought within 30 days. Gun sellers, especially private sellers and the firearms industry, would face reduced sales volume and new reporting duties. Taxpayers would fund a new federal licensing bureaucracy, including offices in urban and rural areas.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun owners, sellers, and the firearms industry

drawbacks.text: The requirement is unusually strict: each license would allow the purchase of a single firearm within 30 days, so a law-abiding owner buying several guns — or replacing one quickly for self-defense — would repeat the full training-and-investigation process each time.

The Attorney General could deny a license based on a broad discretionary list of factors — including drug or alcohol abuse history, animal cruelty offenses, and 'recent acquisition of firearms' — using a 'significant danger' standard that critics would argue is vague and could sweep in people with no disqualifying record.

Gun rights groups and many gun owners oppose licensing-and-permit schemes on the grounds that they condition the exercise of a constitutional right on government permission, delay, and fees; the per-purchase license design would invite legal challenges and political opposition that a universal background check alone would not.

Private individuals would be barred from transferring a firearm directly even to a neighbor or family member without routing it through a licensed dealer, adding cost and friction to ordinary, legal transfers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A federal licensing system with demonstrated safe-handling competence and a danger standard has real potential to keep guns away from people at high risk of harming themselves or others, and it would cover states that have no licensing of their own. The costs are also real: the one-license-per-gun rule, repeated testing for every purchase, and mandatory dealer processing of all private transfers impose significant burdens on law-abiding buyers that go beyond what most state licensing laws require. A narrower design — a standing five-year license rather than a per-purchase permit — would have achieved much of the safety aim at far less cost to ordinary owners; the bill as written stacks maximum friction on every transaction.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 1, 2023, by Rep. Andy Kim of New Jersey and referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote — through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted a single cosponsor, one House Democrat, and no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms sellers, manufacturers, and gun owners who prefer no licensing are better off, because the current rules — no license needed to buy a gun, and private sales with no dealer involvement — continue unchanged. Nothing about the outcome improves safety for anyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun sellers and owners opposed to licensing

for.name: Rep. Andy Kim
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded no further action; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on introduction day.

for.name: 1 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: One House Democrat cosponsored the bill; no others signed on.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup, leaving it without action for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and no Republican support recorded; with 216 House Democrats and 224 House Republicans, that is a near-party-line pattern of Democratic-only backing, though the tiny number of supporters makes the split hard to read.

industries.note: Universal licensing would add a step to every sale, and all private sales would have to be routed through a licensed dealer, cutting into the volume and ease of transactions that drive seller revenue. Sellers' interest in unrestricted sales runs against the bill's aim of keeping guns from high-risk buyers.

Because the bill requires every private firearm transfer to be processed by a licensed dealer with full background-check compliance, it would funnel a new stream of fee-paying transactions to dealers. Dealers gain mandated business, which also serves the bill's public-safety purpose.

A license required for each single-gun purchase, with testing and a 30-day window, would raise the cost and delay of every acquisition and likely reduce unit sales. Manufacturers' interest in high sales volume runs against the bill's restrictions.

industries.industry: Gun owners and sporting shooters' organizations
industries.note: Owners would bear fees, training, fingerprinting, and repeated background investigations for each purchase. Many owners and their organizations treat this as a burden on a constitutional right; public-safety advocates view the same requirements as the point of the bill.
